faq.a: Its blood supply enters distally; a fracture can cut this flow, leading to avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
Lunate dislocation often causes median nerve symptoms and a visible ‘spilled coffee‑bean’ sign on lateral X‑ray, whereas scaphoid fracture shows tenderness in the snuffbox without nerve signs.
faq.q: How can I differentiate a lunate dislocation from a scaphoid fracture?

ai.title: Carpal Bones Anatomy and Clinical Relevance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The eight carpal bones form two rows that enable wrist motion and transmit forces. Understanding their anatomy helps diagnose fractures, dislocations, and systemic diseases that affect bone health in low‑resource settings.

b: Proximal row: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform
Distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate
sections.p: The carpus consists of eight irregular bones arranged in a proximal (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform) and distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate). They articulate with the radius, ulna, and metacarpals, forming the wrist joint.

b: Scaphoid spans proximal and distal rows
Pisiform sits within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon
sections.p: The proximal row sits on the distal radius and ulna; the distal row rests on the bases of the metacarpals. The scaphoid bridges both rows, making it a keystone for wrist stability.

b: Ulnar nerve passes superficial to pisiform
sections.p: Anteriorly the carpal tunnel (median nerve, flexor tendons) lies over the distal row. Posteriorly the extensor compartments pass over the dorsal carpal surface. The ulnar artery and nerve run near the pisiform and triquetrum.

b: Scaphoid: dorsal carpal branch of radial artery
Lunate: dorsal and palmar branches of ulnar artery
sections.p: Each bone receives segmental arterial branches from the radial and ulnar arteries. The scaphoid’s retrograde blood flow from distal to proximal makes the proximal pole vulnerable to avascular necrosis after fracture.
Sensory innervation of the wrist capsule derives from the median, ulnar, and radial nerves, mirroring the distribution of the overlying skin.
The carpal bones permit flexion, extension, radial and ulnar deviation, and a small amount of circumduction, allowing hand positioning for grasp and fine motor tasks.

b: Scaphoid fracture: pain in anatomical snuffbox, risk of AVN
Lunate dislocation: acute wrist pain, median nerve palsy
Pisiform fracture: ulnar‑side tenderness, often missed on X‑ray
sections.p: Fractures of the scaphoid, lunate dislocation, and pisiform sprain are common in low‑resource settings where protective gear is scarce. Systemic bone disease (e.g., HIV‑associated osteopenia, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion) can predispose to atypical fractures.

t.b: Detects obvious fractures; if negative but suspicion high, proceed to CT or MRI
Assesses scaphoid vascularity; confirms occult fracture
Defines fracture lines for surgical planning

b: Positive Tinel’s over carpal tunnel → median nerve compression
sections.p: At the bedside, palpate the anatomical snuffbox for scaphoid tenderness, test wrist range of motion, and assess median nerve function (thumb opposition, sensation).

whenToSeekHelp: Severe wrist swelling with loss of sensation in the thumb and index finger (possible compartment syndrome or lunate dislocation)
Progressive pain despite immobilisation (suspect AVN of scaphoid)
Fever, swelling, and erythema over the wrist in an immunocompromised patient (possible osteomyelitis)
